claim: The abscission of floral organs and emergence of lateral roots in Arabidopsis is regulated by the peptide ligand inflorescence deficient in abscission (IDA) and the receptor protein kinases HAESA (HAE) and HAESA-like 2 (HSL2).
source: The abscission of floral organs and emergence of lateral roots in Arabidopsis is regulated by the peptide ligand inflorescence deficient in abscission (IDA) and the receptor protein kinases HAESA (HAE) and HAESA-like 2 (HSL2).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript (Butenko et al., 2003; Cho et al., 2008; Stenvik et al., 2008; Kumpf et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2016; Santiago et al., 2016).

claim: During cell separation processes, the plant induces defense-associated genes to protect against pathogen invasion.
source: During these cell separation processes, the plant induces defense-associated genes to protect against pathogen invasion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2013) and is a known phenomenon in plant biology.

claim: IDA induces a release of cytosolic calcium ions (Ca2+).
source: Here, we show that IDA induces a release of cytosolic calcium ions (Ca2+) and apoplastic production of reactive oxygen species, which are signatures of early defense responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2, where R-GECO1 and Aequorin sensors were used to measure calcium responses.

claim: IDA induces apoplastic production of reactive oxygen species.
source: Here, we show that IDA induces a release of cytosolic calcium ions (Ca2+) and apoplastic production of reactive oxygen species, which are signatures of early defense responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing ROS production in response to mIDA treatment, and by previous work (Butenko et al., 2014).

claim: IDA promotes late defense responses by the transcriptional upregulation of genes known to be involved in immunity.
source: In addition, we find that IDA promotes late defense responses by the transcriptional upregulation of genes known to be involved in immunity.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 5 and 6 demonstrating upregulation of FRK1, MYB51, and PEP3.

claim: The IDA protein shares a conserved C-terminal domain with the other 7 IDA-like (IDL) members.
source: The IDA protein shares a conserved C-terminal domain with the other 7 IDA-like (IDL) members (Butenko et al., 2003; Vie et al., 2015) which is processed to a functional 12 amino acid hydroxylated peptide (Butenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Butenko et al., 2003; Vie et al., 2015; Butenko et al., 2014).

claim: The IDA C-terminal domain is processed to a functional 12 amino acid hydroxylated peptide.
source: The IDA protein shares a conserved C-terminal domain with the other 7 IDA-like (IDL) members (Butenko et al., 2003; Vie et al., 2015) which is processed to a functional 12 amino acid hydroxylated peptide (Butenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Butenko et al., 2014).

claim: IDA binding to HAE and HSL2 promotes receptor association with members of the co-receptor somatic embryogenesis receptor kinase (SERK) family.
source: IDA binding to HAE and HSL2 promotes receptor association with members of the co-receptor somatic embryogenesis receptor kinase (SERK) family and further downstream signaling leading to cell separation events. (Cho et al., 2008; Meng et al., 2016; Santiago et al., 2016; Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Cho et al., 2008; Meng et al., 2016; Santiago et al., 2016; Stenvik et al., 2008).

claim: IDA and IDL family members bind and activate HSL1 in the regulation of leaf epidermal patterning.
source: Recently, it has been shown that IDA and IDL family members also bind and activate HSL1 in the regulation of leaf epidermal pattering, indicating subfunctionalisation within this clade of receptors (Roman et al., 2022) and opens for the possibility that HAE or HSL2 could have additional functions than regulating cell separation events.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work (Roman et al., 2022).

claim: A deficiency in the IDA signaling pathway prevents the expression of genes encoding secreted cell wall remodeling and hydrolase enzymes thus hindering floral organs to abscise.
source: A deficiency in the IDA signaling pathway prevents the expression of genes encoding secreted cell wall remodeling and hydrolase enzymes thus hindering floral organs to abscise (Butenko et al., 2003; Cho et al., 2008; Kumpf et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2016; Niederhuth et al., 2013; Stenvik et al., 2008; Taylor and Walker, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Butenko et al., 2003; Cho et al., 2008; Kumpf et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2016; Niederhuth et al., 2013; Stenvik et al., 2008; Taylor and Walker, 2018).

claim: IDA signaling through HAE and HSL2 regulates cell wall remodeling genes in the endodermal, cortical, and epidermal tissues overlaying the LR primordia during LR emergence.
source: IDA signaling through HAE and HSL2 regulates cell wall remodeling genes in the endodermal, cortical, and epidermal tissues overlaying the LR primordia during LR emergence (Kumpf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kumpf et al., 2013).

claim: IDL1 signals through HSL2 to regulate cell separation during root cap sloughing.
source: In addition, IDL1 signals through HSL2 to regulate cell separation during root cap sloughing (Shi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Shi et al., 2018).

claim: AZ cells undergoing cell separation express defense genes that function in protecting the AZ cells from infection after abscission has occurred.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that AZ cells undergoing cell separation express defense genes and it has been proposed that they function in protecting the AZ cells from infection after abscission has occurred (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2013).

claim: IDA elicits the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in Nicotiana benthamiana (N. benthamiana) leaves transiently expressing the HAE or HSL2 receptor.
source: IDA elicits the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in Nicotiana benthamiana (N. benthamiana) leaves transiently expressing the HAE or HSL2 receptor (Butenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Butenko et al., 2014).

claim: ROS occurs in the apoplast and is involved in regulating the cell wall structure by producing cross-linking of cell wall components in the form of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) or act as cell wall loosening agents in the form of hydroxyl radical (·OH) radicals.
source: As a consequence of defense responses, ROS occurs in the apoplast and is involved in regulating the cell wall structure by producing cross-linking of cell wall components in the form of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) or act as cell wall loosening agents in the form of hydroxyl radical (·OH) radicals (Kärkönen and Kuchitsu, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kärkönen and Kuchitsu, 2015).

claim: ROS may serve as a direct defense response by their highly reactive and toxic properties.
source: ROS may also serve as a direct defense response by their highly reactive and toxic properties (Kärkönen and Kuchitsu, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kärkönen and Kuchitsu, 2015).

claim: ROS may act as a secondary signaling molecule enhancing intracellular defense responses as well as contributing to the induction of defense-related genes.
source: In addition, ROS may act as a secondary signaling molecule enhancing intracellular defense responses as well as contributing to the induction of defense-related genes (reviewed in Castro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review (Castro et al., 2021).

claim: Apoplastic ROS is mainly produced by a family of NADPH oxidases located in the PM known as respiratory burst oxidase proteins (RBOHs).
source: In Arabidopsis, apoplastic ROS is mainly produced by a family of NADPH oxidases located in the PM known as respiratory burst oxidase proteins (RBOHs; Torres and Dangl, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Torres and Dangl, 2005).

claim: The production of ROS is often found closely linked to an increase in the concentration of cytosolic Ca2+ ([Ca2+]cyt).
source: The production of ROS is often found closely linked to an increase in the concentration of cytosolic Ca2+ ([Ca2+]cyt), where the interplay between these signaling molecules is observed in immunity across kingdoms (Kadota et al., 2015; Steinhorst and Kudla, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Kadota et al., 2015; Steinhorst and Kudla, 2013).

claim: ROS and [Ca2+]cyt are known signaling molecules acting downstream of several peptide ligand-receptor pairs.
source: Interestingly, ROS and [Ca2+]cyt are known signaling molecules acting downstream of several peptide ligand-receptor pairs.
evidence: This is supported by the context and citations to work on PEP peptides and flg22 (Huffaker et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2010; Felix et al., 1999; Gómez-Gómez et al., 1999; Ranf et al., 2011).

claim: The endogenous PAMPs elicitor peptide (PEP)1, PEP2, and PEP3 function as elicitors of systemic responses against pathogen attack and herbivory.
source: This includes the endogenous PAMPs elicitor peptide (PEP)1, PEP2, and PEP3 which function as elicitors of systemic responses against pathogen attack and herbivory (Huffaker et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2010), as well as the pathogen derived peptide ligands flagellin22 (flg22) and elongation factor thermo unstable (Ef-Tu) which bind and activate defense-related RKs in the PM of the plant cell (Felix et al., 1999; Gómez-Gómez et al., 1999; Ranf et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Huffaker et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2010).

claim: The pathogen derived peptide ligands flagellin22 (flg22) and elongation factor thermo unstable (Ef-Tu) bind and activate defense-related RKs in the PM of the plant cell.
source: This includes the endogenous PAMPs elicitor peptide (PEP)1, PEP2, and PEP3 which function as elicitors of systemic responses against pathogen attack and herbivory (Huffaker et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2010), as well as the pathogen derived peptide ligands flagellin22 (flg22) and elongation factor thermo unstable (Ef-Tu) which bind and activate defense-related RKs in the PM of the plant cell (Felix et al., 1999; Gómez-Gómez et al., 1999; Ranf et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Felix et al., 1999; Gómez-Gómez et al., 1999; Ranf et al., 2011).

claim: The flg22 peptide interacts with the extracellular domain of the flagellin sensing 2 (FLS2) receptor kinase, which rapidly leads to an increase in [Ca2+]cyt.
source: The flg22 peptide interacts with the extracellular domain of the flagellin sensing 2 (FLS2) receptor kinase, which rapidly leads to an increase in [Ca2+]cyt (Ranf et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Ranf et al., 2011).

claim: In a resting state, the co-receptor brassinosteroid insensitive1-associated receptor kinase 1/SERK3 (BAK1) and the cytoplasmic kinase botrytis-induced kinase 1 (BIK1) form a complex with FLS2.
source: In a resting state, the co-receptor brassinosteroid insensitive1-associated receptor kinase 1/SERK3 (BAK1) and the cytoplasmic kinase botrytis-induced kinase 1 (BIK1) form a complex with FLS2.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to work on FLS2 signaling (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).

claim: Upon binding of flg22 to the FLS2 receptor, BIK1 is released from the receptor complex and activates intracellular signaling molecules through phosphorylation, among other, the PM localized RBOHD.
source: Upon binding of flg22 to the FLS2 receptor, BIK1 is released from the receptor complex and activates intracellular signaling molecules through phosphorylation, among other, the PM localized RBOHD (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).

claim: The flg22-induced apoplastic ROS produced binds to PM localized Ca2+ channels on neighboring cells, activating Ca2+ influx into the cytosol.
source: The flg22-induced apoplastic ROS produced binds to PM localized Ca2+ channels on neighboring cells, activating Ca2+ influx into the cytosol.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ROS-Ca2+ signaling, supported by the context and citation to Dubiella et al., 2013.

claim: The cytosolic Ca2+ may bind to calcium-dependent protein kinase5 (CDPKs) regulating RBOHD activity through phosphorylation.
source: The cytosolic Ca2+ may bind to calcium-dependent protein kinase5 (CDPKs) regulating RBOHD activity through phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Ca2+-dependent signaling, supported by citation to Dubiella et al., 2013.

claim: The Ca2+-dependent phosphorylation of RBOH enhances ROS production, which in turn leads to a propagation of the ROS/Ca2+ signal through the plant tissue.
source: The Ca2+-dependent phosphorylation of RBOH enhances ROS production, which in turn leads to a propagation of the ROS/Ca2+ signal through the plant tissue (Dubiella et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Dubiella et al., 2013).

claim: A rapid increase in [Ca2+]cyt is observed in response to developmental signals, such as extracellular auxin and environmental signals, such as high-salt conditions and drought.
source: A rapid increase in [Ca2+]cyt is not only observed in peptide-ligand-induced signaling. Similar [Ca2+]cyt changes are observed as responses to developmental signals, such as extracellular auxin and environmental signals, such as high-salt conditions and drought (reviewed in Kudla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review (Kudla et al., 2018).

claim: [Ca2+]cyt signals are observed in single cells during pollen tube and root hair growth.
source: Also, [Ca2+]cyt signals are observed in single cells during pollen tube and root hair growth (Monshausen et al., 2008; Sanders et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Monshausen et al., 2008; Sanders et al., 1999).

claim: The cell contains a large toolkit of Ca2+ sensor proteins that may affect cellular function through changes in protein phosphorylation and gene expression.
source: How cells decipher the [Ca2+]cyt changes into a specific cellular response is still largely unknown, however, the cell contains a large toolkit of Ca2+ sensor proteins that may affect cellular function through changes in protein phosphorylation and gene expression.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to work on Ca2+ sensors (Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012).

claim: Each Ca2+ binding protein has specific affinities for Ca2+ allowing them to respond to different Ca2+ concentrations providing a specific cellular response.
source: Each Ca2+ binding protein has specific affinities for Ca2+ allowing them to respond to different Ca2+ concentrations providing a specific cellular response (Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012).

claim: mIDA elicits extracellular ROS in hae hsl2 35S:HAE-YFP leaf discs treated with mIDA.
source: hae hsl2 35 S:HAE-YFP leaf discs treated with mIDA emitted extracellular ROS, whereas no response was observed in wild-type (WT) leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-c using a luminol-dependent ROS assay.

claim: No ROS response was observed in wild-type (WT) leaves treated with mIDA.
source: hae hsl2 35 S:HAE-YFP leaf discs treated with mIDA emitted extracellular ROS, whereas no response was observed in wild-type (WT) leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: There is a decrease in HAE and HSL2 promoter activity in the oldest rosette leaves.
source: We investigated the activity of the HAE and HSL2 promoter in 22 days old Arabidopsis rosette leaves by cloning the promoters fused to the nuclear localized YFP-derived fluorophore Venus protein (pHAE:Venus-H2B, pHSL2:Venus-H2B) and could observe a decrease in promoter activity in the oldest rosette leaves giving a possible explanation to the lack of mIDA induced ROS in true leaves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e using promoter-reporter constructs.

claim: Following application of 1 μM mIDA, an increase in [Ca2+]cyt was detected in 10-day-old roots expressing R-GECO1.
source: Following application of 1 μM mIDA, we detected an increase in [Ca2+]cyt (Figure 1a and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a using the R-GECO1 calcium sensor.

claim: The mIDA-induced Ca2+ response starts 4–5 min after application of the mIDA peptide and lasts for 7–8 min.
source: R-GECO1 fluorescence intensities normalized to background intensities (ΔF/F) were measured from a region of interest (ROI) covering the meristematic and elongation zone of the root and revealed that the response starts 4–5 min after application of the mIDA peptide and lasts for 7–8 min (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a measuring R-GECO1 fluorescence over time.

claim: The mIDA-induced Ca2+ signal initiated in the root meristematic zone from where it spread toward the elongation zone and root tip.
source: The signal initiated in the root meristematic zone from where it spread toward the elongation zone and root tip, a second wave was observed in the meristematic zone continuing with Ca2+ spikes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and the heat map showing spatial distribution of the Ca2+ signal.

claim: The mIDA-induced Ca2+ signal amplitude was at a maximum within the elongation zone and decreased as the signal spread.
source: The signal amplitude was at a maximum within the elongation zone and decreased as the signal spread (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The flg22-induced Ca2+ signal initiated in the root elongation zone from where it spread toward the meristematic zone as a single wave.
source: Analysis of roots treated with 1 μM flg22 showed that the Ca2+ signal initiated in the root elongation zone from where it spread toward the meristematic zone as a single wave and that the signal amplitude was at a maximum within the elongation zone and decreased as the signal spread (Figure 1b, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b using the R-GECO1 calcium sensor.

claim: The flg22-induced Ca2+ signal amplitude was at a maximum within the elongation zone and decreased as the signal spread.
source: Analysis of roots treated with 1 μM flg22 showed that the Ca2+ signal initiated in the root elongation zone from where it spread toward the meristematic zone as a single wave and that the signal amplitude was at a maximum within the elongation zone and decreased as the signal spread (Figure 1b, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: There are differences in tissue specificity of Ca2+ responses between mIDA and flg22.
source: These observations indicate differences in tissue specificity of Ca2+ responses between mIDA and flg22, which we hypothesize depend on the cellular distribution of their cognate receptors.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observed differences in Ca2+ signal patterns shown in Figures 1a and 1b.

claim: pHAE:Venus-H2B lines had fluorescent expression in the epidermis and stele of the elongation zone.
source: pHAE:Venus-H2B lines had fluorescent expression in the epidermis and stele of the elongation zone (Figure 1c)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c using promoter-reporter constructs.

claim: pHSL2:Venus-H2B lines had fluorescent expression in the lateral root cap, root tip and root meristem.
source: pHSL2:Venus-H2B lines in the lateral root cap, root tip and root meristem (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d using promoter-reporter constructs.

claim: Fluorescent nuclei were observed in the stele of the elongation zone in pFLS2:Venus-H2B lines.
source: while fluorescent nuclei were observed in the stele of the elongation zone in pFLS2:Venus-H2B lines (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e using promoter-reporter constructs.

claim: The different patterns of fluorescent nuclei observed for the three different receptor constructs could explain the differences in the Ca2+ signatures triggered by mIDA and flg22.
source: The different patterns of fluorescent nuclei observed for the three different receptor constructs could indeed explain the differences in the Ca2+ signatures triggered by mIDA and flg22.
evidence: This is based on inference from the promoter activity data (Figures 1c-e) and the Ca2+ response data (Figures 1a-b).

claim: Seven days old Aeq-Seedlings treated with 1 μM IDAΔN69 did not show any increase in [Ca2+]cyt.
source: Seven days old Aeq-Seedlings treated with 1 μM IDAΔN69 did not show any increase in [Ca2+]cyt (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a using the Aequorin calcium sensor.

claim: The mIDA induced response was abolished in Aeq-seedlings pre-incubated in 2 mM EGTA or 1 mM LaCL3.
source: The mIDA induced response was abolished in Aeq-seedlings pre-incubated in 2 mM EGTA or 1 mM LaCL3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b), indicating that the mIDA dependent [Ca2+]cyt response depends on Ca2+ from the extracellular space.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b using calcium channel inhibitors.

claim: The mIDA dependent [Ca2+]cyt response depends on Ca2+ from the extracellular space.
source: The mIDA induced response was abolished in Aeq-seedlings pre-incubated in 2 mM EGTA or 1 mM LaCL3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b), indicating that the mIDA dependent [Ca2+]cyt response depends on Ca2+ from the extracellular space.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing that calcium channel blockers and chelators abolish the mIDA response (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).

claim: Only flowers at the stage where there is an initial weakening of the AZ cell walls showed an increase in [Ca2+]cyt in response to mIDA.
source: Interestingly, only flowers at the stage where there is an initial weakening of the AZ cell walls showed an increase in [Ca2+]cyt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 using the Aequorin calcium sensor in flowers at different developmental stages.

claim: Flowers treated with mIDA prior to cell wall loosening showed no increase in luminescence.
source: Flowers treated with mIDA prior to cell wall loosening showed no increase in luminescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the mIDA-triggered Ca2+ release in flowers correlates with the onset of the abscission process and the increase in HAE and HSL2 expression at the AZ (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Patharkar and Walker, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mIDA-triggered Ca2+ release in flowers correlates with the onset of the abscission process and the increase in HAE and HSL2 expression at the AZ.
source: Flowers treated with mIDA prior to cell wall loosening showed no increase in luminescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the mIDA-triggered Ca2+ release in flowers correlates with the onset of the abscission process and the increase in HAE and HSL2 expression at the AZ (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Patharkar and Walker, 2015).
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and citations to previous work (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Patharkar and Walker, 2015).

claim: The Ca2+ signal in flowers at position 6 was composed of one wave that initiated close to the nectaries and spread throughout the AZ and further into the floral receptacle.
source: The AZ region was analyzed for signal intensity values and revealed that the Ca2+ signal was composed of one wave (Figure 2, Figure 2—video 1). The signal initiated close to the nectaries and spread throughout the AZ and further into the floral receptacle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 using the R-GECO1 calcium sensor in flowers.

claim: Flowers treated with 1 μM IDAΔN69 did not show any increase in [Ca2+]cyt in the AZ or receptacle.
source: Flowers treated with 1 μM IDAΔN69 did not show any increase in [Ca2+]cyt in the AZ or receptacle, while a clear Ca2+ wave could be detected in the whole AZ, receptacle and proximal pedicel after treatment with eATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A clear Ca2+ wave could be detected in the whole AZ, receptacle and proximal pedicel after treatment with eATP.
source: Flowers treated with 1 μM IDAΔN69 did not show any increase in [Ca2+]cyt in the AZ or receptacle, while a clear Ca2+ wave could be detected in the whole AZ, receptacle and proximal pedicel after treatment with eATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: HAE and HSL2 promoter activity in flowers at position 6 shows restricted promoter activity to the AZ cells.
source: Detailed investigation of HAE and HSL2 promoter activity in flowers at position 6 shows restricted promoter activity to the AZ cells (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b using promoter-reporter constructs.

claim: The observed HAE and HSL2 promoter activity correlates with the observed mIDA-induced [Ca2+]cyt response in flowers.
source: The observed promoter activity correlates with the observed mIDA-induced [Ca2+]cyt response.
evidence: This is based on inference from comparing the promoter activity data (Figure 2b) with the Ca2+ response data (Figure 2).

claim: Plants carrying mutations in the CNGCs genes expressed in AZs showed no defect in floral organ abscission.
source: We observed no deficiency in floral abscission in the cngc mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 4b), in contrast to what is observed in the hae hsl2 mutant where all floral organs are retained throughout the inflorescence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4b showing normal abscission in cngc mutants.

claim: RBOHD and RBOHF have high transcriptional levels in the floral AZs.
source: Two members of this family, RBOHD and RBOHF have high transcriptional levels in the floral AZs (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 4a, Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008) and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a.

claim: ROS was observed in both WT and to a lower extent in rbohd rbohdf flowers treated with H2DCF-DA.
source: We treated AZs with the ROS indicator, H2DCF-DA, which upon contact with ROS has fluorescent properties, and observed ROS in both WT and to a lower extent in rbohd rbohdf flowers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4c using the H2DCF-DA ROS indicator.

claim: Normal floral abscission was observed in the rbohd rbohf double mutant flowers.
source: In addition, we observed normal floral abscission in the rbohd rbohf double mutant flowers, indicating that the developmental progression of cell separation is not dependent on RBOHD and RBOHF (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4c and d.

claim: The developmental progression of cell separation is not dependent on RBOHD and RBOHF.
source: In addition, we observed normal floral abscission in the rbohd rbohf double mutant flowers, indicating that the developmental progression of cell separation is not dependent on RBOHD and RBOHF (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c and d).
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation of normal abscission in rbohd rbohf mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c and d).

claim: The rbohd rbohf mutant showed a significant lower pBS value compared to WT at the developmental stage where cell loosening normally occurs, indicating premature cell wall loosening.
source: Measurements showed a significant lower pBS value for the rbohd rbohf mutant compared to WT at the developmental stage where cell loosening normally occurs, indicating premature cell wall loosening (Figure 2—figure supplement 4e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4e using petal break strength measurements.

claim: rbohd rbohf petals abscised one position earlier than WT.
source: Furthermore, rbohd rbohf petals abscised one position earlier than WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 4e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4e.

claim: Infection with the pathogen P. syringae induces cauline leaf abscission in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, infection with the pathogen P. syringae induces cauline leaf abscission.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Patharkar et al., 2017; Patharkar and Walker, 2016).

claim: Stress induced cauline leaf abscission was reduced in plants with mutations in components of the IDA-HAE/HSL2 signaling pathway.
source: Interestingly, stress induced cauline leaf abscission was reduced in plants with mutations in components of the IDA-HAE/HSL2 signaling pathway (Patharkar et al., 2017; Patharkar and Walker, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Patharkar et al., 2017; Patharkar and Walker, 2016).

claim: Upregulation of defense genes in floral AZ cells during the abscission process is altered in the hae hsl2 mutant.
source: In addition, upregulation of defense genes in floral AZ cells during the abscission process is altered in the hae hsl2 mutant (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2013), indicating that the IDA-HAE/HSL2 signaling system may be involved in regulating defense responses in cells undergoing cell separation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Cai and Lashbrook, 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2013).

claim: pIDA:GUS seedlings exposed to flg22 showed a significant increase in GUS expression in LR primordia compared to control seedlings.
source: Compared to the control seedlings, the seedlings exposed to flg22 and chitin showed a significant increase in GUS expression in LR primordia (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a using pIDA:GUS reporter lines.

claim: pIDA:GUS seedlings exposed to chitin showed a significant increase in GUS expression in LR primordia compared to control seedlings.
source: Compared to the control seedlings, the seedlings exposed to flg22 and chitin showed a significant increase in GUS expression in LR primordia (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a using pIDA:GUS reporter lines.

claim: A GUS signal was observed in the primary root of flg22 and chitin treated roots but not in untreated root tips.
source: Also, when comparing untreated root tips to those exposed to flg22 and chitin we observed a GUS signal in the primary root of flg22 and chitin treated roots (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b using pIDA:GUS reporter lines.

claim: A significant increase in fluorescence was observed for flg22 and chitin treated samples compared to untreated controls using the 4-MUG fluorogenic GUS assay.
source: A significant increase in fluorescence was observed for flg22 and chitin treated samples compared to untreated controls, (Figure 3b), which was not observed when exposing seedlings to IDAΔN69 indicating that increased IDA expression is not triggered simply by the application of a peptide (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and 3c using the fluorogenic GUS assay.

claim: No significant increase in fluorescence was observed when exposing seedlings to IDAΔN69, indicating that increased IDA expression is not triggered simply by the application of a peptide.
source: A significant increase in fluorescence was observed for flg22 and chitin treated samples compared to untreated controls, (Figure 3b), which was not observed when exposing seedlings to IDAΔN69 indicating that increased IDA expression is not triggered simply by the application of a peptide (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing no response to IDAΔN69 (Figure 3c).

claim: When pIDA:GUS seedlings were treated with mannitol or NaCl, an increment in GUS signal was observed surrounding the LR primordia.
source: When pIDA:GUS seedling were treated with the osmotic agent mannitol or exposed to salt stress by NaCl, both treatments simulating dry soil, a similar increment in GUS signal was observed surrounding the LR primordia (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a using pIDA:GUS reporter lines.

claim: No pIDA:GUS expression was detected in the primary root when seedlings were treated with mannitol or NaCl.
source: However, no pIDA:GUS expression was detected in the primary root (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: An increase in the callose depositions per area upon mIDA treatment compared to water treated controls was observed in 35S:HAE-YFP lines.
source: An increase in the callose depositions per area upon mIDA treatment compared to water treated controls was observed in these lines (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and b using callose staining.

claim: No difference in callose deposition was detected in WT seedlings treated with mIDA compared to water treated controls.
source: We detected no difference to water treated controls indicating that either callose deposition is not a cellular outcome for mIDA treatment (Figure 4a and b), or that receptor availability in the cotyledons is too low to observe a response
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: flg22-treated WT seedlings showed increased callose deposition.
source: As a control, flg22-treated WT seedlings showed increased callose deposition, which was not observed in flg22-treated fls2 seedlings (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: Increased callose deposition was not observed in flg22-treated fls2 seedlings.
source: As a control, flg22-treated WT seedlings showed increased callose deposition, which was not observed in flg22-treated fls2 seedlings (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: mIDA is capable of promoting a HAE-dependent deposition of callose as a long-term defense response.
source: These results indicate that mIDA, is capable of promoting a HAE-dependent deposition of callose as a long-term defense response.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing callose deposition in 35S:HAE-YFP lines but not in WT (Figure 4).

claim: FRK1 is a specific and early immune-responsive gene activated by multiple MAMPs.
source: FLG22-induced receptor-like kinase1 (FRK1), a specific and early immune-responsive gene activated by multiple MAMPs (Asai et al., 2002; He et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Asai et al., 2002; He et al., 2006).

claim: MYB51 is a WRKY target gene previously shown to increase in response to the MAMP flg22 resulting in biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite indolic glucosinolates.
source: MYB51, a WRKY target gene, previously shown to increase in response to the MAMP flg22 (Frerigmann et al., 2016) resulting in biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite indolic glucosinolates
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Frerigmann et al., 2016).

claim: All defense-associated marker genes (FRK1, MYB51, PEP3) showed a significant transcriptional elevation 1 hr after mIDA treatment in WT seedlings.
source: All genes showed a significant transcriptional elevation 1 hr after mIDA treatment (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a using RT-qPCR.

claim: After 12 h, FRK1 and PEP3 transcription in mIDA-treated tissue was not significantly different from untreated tissue.
source: After 12 h, FRK1 and PEP3 transcription in mIDA-treated tissue was not significantly different from untreated tissue, whereas transcription of MYB51 in mIDA-treated tissue remained elevated after 12 hr but was significantly lower compared to 1 hr after mIDA treatment (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a using RT-qPCR.

claim: Transcription of MYB51 in mIDA-treated tissue remained elevated after 12 hr but was significantly lower compared to 1 hr after mIDA treatment.
source: After 12 h, FRK1 and PEP3 transcription in mIDA-treated tissue was not significantly different from untreated tissue, whereas transcription of MYB51 in mIDA-treated tissue remained elevated after 12 hr but was significantly lower compared to 1 hr after mIDA treatment (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a using RT-qPCR.

claim: The observed increase in transcription of the defense genes MYB51 and PEP3 was only partially reduced in the hae hsl2 mutant.
source: Interestingly, the observed increase in transcription of the defense genes MYB51 and PEP3, was only partially reduced in the hae hsl2 mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 using RT-qPCR.

claim: FRK1 showed higher transcriptional levels in the hae hsl2 mutant compared to WT after mIDA treatment.
source: In contrast, FRK1 showed higher transcriptional levels in the hae hsl2 mutant compared to WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 using RT-qPCR.

claim: Other receptors than HAE and HSL2 are involved in the mIDA-induced enhancement of the defense genes FRK1, MYB51, and PEP3.
source: These results indicate that also other receptors than HAE and HSL2 are involved in the mIDA-induced enhancement of the defense genes FRK1, MYB51, and PEP3.
evidence: This is based on inference from the observation that defense gene induction is only partially reduced in hae hsl2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Enhanced expression of pMYB51:YFPN was predominantly detected in the meristematic zone of the root after 7 hr of mIDA treatment.
source: Enhanced expression of pMYB51:YFPN was predominantly detected in the meristematic zone of the root after 7 hr of mIDA treatment, compared to a non-treated control (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b using a promoter-reporter line.

claim: Comparison of mIDA induction with the elicitor-triggered response of pMYB51:YFPN to flg22 showed similar temporal expression in the root.
source: Moreover, comparison of mIDA induction with the elicitor-triggered response of pMYB51:YFPN to flg22 showed similar temporal expression in the root (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The relative increase in transcription of FRK1, MYB51, and PEP3 is similar when seedlings are treated with mIDA and flg22.
source: The relative increase in transcription of the genes tested is similar when seedlings are treated with mIDA and flg22 (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a using RT-qPCR.

claim: When treating seedlings with both mIDA and flg22, the relative transcription of FRK1, MYB51, and PEP3 increased substantially.
source: However, when treating seedlings with both peptides the relative transcription of the genes of interest increased substantially.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a using RT-qPCR.

claim: The combined enhanced transcription when seedlings were co-treated with both flg22 and mIDA exceeds a simple additive effect of the two peptides.
source: To our surprise, the combined enhanced transcription when seedling where co-treated with both flg22 and mIDA exceeds a simple additive effect of the two peptides.
evidence: This is based on inference from the RT-qPCR data showing synergistic effects (Figure 6a).

claim: No enhanced transcription of FRK1, MYB51 and PEP3 were observed after co-treatment with PIP1 and mIDA.
source: In contrast to what we observed with flg22, no enhanced transcription of FRK1, MYB51 and PEP3 were observed after co-treatment with PIP1 and mIDA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 using RT-qPCR.

claim: Fluorescent nuclei with overlapping Venus and Tomato expression were observed in the vascular tissue of the root, in cells surrounding LRs as well as in cells of the AZs of plants expressing pFLS2-Venus-H2B and pHAE-Tomato-H2B.
source: Fluorescent nuclei with overlapping Venus and Tomato expression were observed both in the vascular tissue of the root, in cells surrounding LRs as well as in cells of the AZs of plants expressing pFLS2-Venus-H2B and pHAE-Tomat-H2B (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b using dual promoter-reporter lines.

claim: Overlapping fluorescent nuclei in pFLS2-Venus-H2B and pHSL2-Tomato-H2B lines were mainly observed in the epidermal cells surrounding the LR and in the root tip, as well as in the root cap.
source: Similar observations were done in the AZ of lines expressing pFLS2-Venus-H2B and pHSL2-Tomat-H2B lines; however, in these lines overlapping fluorescent nuclei in roots were mainly observed in the epidermal cells surrounding the LR and in the root tip, as well as in the root cap (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c using dual promoter-reporter lines.

claim: IDA plays a role in enhancing immune responses in tissue undergoing cell separation, possibly by enhancing cellular responses activated by immune receptors, such as FLS2.
source: Based on these results, we propose a role for IDA in enhancing immune responses in tissue undergoing cell separation, possibly by enhancing cellular responses activated by immune receptors, such as FLS2.
evidence: This is based on inference from the combined experimental data showing synergistic effects of mIDA and flg22, and overlapping receptor expression patterns.

claim: The mIDA cellular output is similar to that of flg22 yet shows some distinct differences.
source: It is intriguing that the mIDA cellular output is similar to that of flg22 (Kadota et al., 2015; Kadota et al., 2014) yet shows some distinct differences.
evidence: This is based on inference from comparing the experimental data for mIDA and flg22 responses throughout the manuscript.

claim: The spatial distribution of the Ca2+ wave originated by mIDA differs from that of flg22.
source: The spatial distribution of the Ca2+ wave originated by mIDA differs from that of flg22.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1a and 1b comparing Ca2+ responses.

claim: The rbohd rbohf mutant shows ROS production in the AZ, indicating that other NADPH oxidases or cell wall peroxidases expressed in the AZ may be involved in ROS production.
source: The rbohd rbohf mutant shows ROS production in the AZ, indicating that other NADPH oxidases or cell wall peroxidases expressed in the AZ may be involved in ROS production, in contrast to the importance of RBOHD RBOHF in flg22 signaling (Kadota et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing ROS in rbohd rbohf mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c) and citation to previous work (Kadota et al., 2015).

claim: IDA and flg22 share many components for their signal transduction, such as the BAK1 co-receptor and MAPK cascade.
source: This suggests that while IDA and flg22 share many components for their signal transduction, such as the BAK1 co-receptor (Chinchilla et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2016) and MAPK cascade (Asai et al., 2002; Cho et al., 2008), there are other specific components that are likely important to provide differences in signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Chinchilla et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2016; Asai et al., 2002; Cho et al., 2008).

claim: FLS2 arrangement into nanoscale domains at the PM is dependent on FER.
source: Interestingly, FLS2 arrangement into nanoscale domains at the PM is dependent on FER. FLS2 becomes more disperse and mobile in fer mutants, implying a role for FER in regulating FLS2 activity (Gronnier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Gronnier et al., 2022).

claim: Altering of the cell wall affects FLS2 nanoscale organization.
source: Also altering of the cell wall affects FLS2 nanoscale organization (McKenna et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (McKenna et al., 2019).

claim: LRR-RLKs known to play a function in biotic or abiotic stress responses, such as RLK7, are found to interact mainly with HSL2.
source: Interestingly, LRR-RLKs known to play a function in biotic or abiotic stress responses, such as receptor-like kinase 7 (RLK7), strubbelig-receptor family 3, receptor-like protein kinase 1 and FRK1, are found to interact mainly with HSL2, whereas HAE shows interaction with LRRs mainly involved in development (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from a high-throughput interaction assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 (Smakowska-Luzan et al., 2018).

claim: HAE shows interaction with LRRs mainly involved in development.
source: Interestingly, LRR-RLKs known to play a function in biotic or abiotic stress responses, such as receptor-like kinase 7 (RLK7), strubbelig-receptor family 3, receptor-like protein kinase 1 and FRK1, are found to interact mainly with HSL2, whereas HAE shows interaction with LRRs mainly involved in development (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from a high-throughput interaction assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 (Smakowska-Luzan et al., 2018).

claim: RLK7 has been identified as an additional receptor for CEP4, involved in regulating cell surface immunity and response to nitrogen starvation.
source: RLK7 has recently been identified as an additional receptor for CEP4, involved in regulating cell surface immunity and response to nitrogen starvation, indication a role of RLK7 as an additional receptor regulating defense responses in known peptide-receptor complexes (Rzemieniewski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work (Rzemieniewski et al., 2022).

claim: IDA is able to induce an intracellular release of Ca2+ in Arabidopsis root tips as well as in the AZ.
source: Here we report that IDA is able to induce an intracellular release of Ca2+ in Arabidopsis root tips as well as in the AZ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2 using calcium sensors.

claim: A range of biotic and abiotic signals can induce IDA expression.
source: We show that a range of biotic and abiotic signals can induce IDA expression
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 using pIDA:GUS reporter lines.

claim: The IDA signal modulates responses of plant immune signaling.
source: we demonstrate that the IDA signal modulates responses of plant immune signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing IDA effects on defense responses (Figures 4, 5, 6).

claim: In addition to regulating cell separation, IDA plays a role in enhancing a defense response in tissues undergoing cell separation.
source: We propose that, in addition to regulating cell separation, IDA plays a role in enhancing a defense response in tissues undergoing cell separation thus providing the essential need for enhanced defense responses in tissue during the cell separation event.
evidence: This is based on inference from all the experimental data showing IDA's dual role in cell separation and defense.
